case.case_title: Sumanadasa and 205 Others vs. Attorney General
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports (2006) 3 Sri L. R.

clause.text: General restrictions may apply for national security, public order, health, morality, and welfare.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the restriction on bail under Section 47(1) of the Immigration and Emigration Act constitutes a permissible restriction under Article 15(7) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that their fundamental rights under Article 13(2) were infringed due to continuous detention without a remedy, and that Section 47(1) could not validly restrict these rights.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondent argued that the restrictions under Section 47(1) are valid existing law and do not amount to a restriction under Article 13(2), and that any restriction must be based on Article 15(7).
key_facts: Section 47(1) of the Immigration and Emigration Act makes certain offences non-bailable.
Petitioners were detained without bail under this provision.
The Court of Appeal dismissed bail applications based on this section.
The petitioners alleged violation of Article 13(2) due to lack of procedure for continued detention.
The Court considered whether Section 47(1) restricts fundamental rights under Article 15(7).

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that any abridgment, restriction or denial of fundamental rights must be based on specific constitutional provisions, and Article 15(7) contains the permitted restrictions. Section 47(1) of the Immigration and Emigration Act could not be construed as restricting the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 13(2).
reasoning.application_to_facts: Since Section 47(1) does not fall within the scope of restrictions permitted by Article 15(7), the continuous detention without a procedure to adjudicate continued detention violates Article 13(2).
principles_established: Restrictions on fundamental rights must be grounded in specific constitutional provisions.
Section 47(1) does not constitute a valid restriction under Article 15(7).
Fundamental rights must be respected, secured, and advanced by all organs of government.

outcome.holding: The Court held that Section 47(1) could not be construed as restricting the fundamental right under Article 13(2) and that the petitioners' rights were infringed.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Magistrate Courts are directed to decide on continued detention according to procedure applicable to non-bailable offences.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 15(7) sets the constitutional framework for permissible restrictions on fundamental rights. The Court analyzed whether the statutory bail restriction fell within these permissible grounds and found it did not, making this clause central to the reasoning and outcome.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: Any abridgment, restriction or denial has to be based only on specific provisions of the Constitution itself, and Article 16(1) does not amount to a specific restricting of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 13(2). The permitted restrictions are contained in Article 15(7) and the provisions of Section 47(1) of the Immigration and Emigration Act could never be construed as restricting fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 13(2).
